corrected_value.title: Atypical cerebral lateralisation in adults with compensated developmental dyslexia demonstrated using functional transcranial Doppler ultrasound

decisions.location: Conclusions, lines 2385-2395 (see also Methods lines 1281-1295; Discussion lines 2183-2189; References lines 2869-2875)
decisions.quote:
In a large sample of twins oversampled for language problems, the present study failed to 

find evidence for atypical laterality, either in terms of handedness or cerebral lateralisation for 

language, in those with DLD. Theories have proposed that disruption to the typical left 

hemisphere dominance for language may be a neurobiological correlate of language problems 

(e.g. Annett, 2002; Bishop, 2013; T. J. Crow et al., 1998), and empirical studies of very small 

samples have supported that view (Illingworth & Bishop, 2009; Whitehouse & Bishop, 2008).
decisions.reason: Prior adjudication and state files are absent for this work. In Methods (lines 1281-1295), the authors explicitly include children impaired on literacy measures in the DLD group on the basis of Illingworth & Bishop's (2009) fTCD finding of reduced left-hemisphere language lateralisation in dyslexia, and in both the Discussion (lines 2183-2189) and Conclusions (lines 2385-2415) they explicitly state that their fTCD comparison failed to replicate the reduced left-hemisphere language dominance reported by Illingworth & Bishop (2009) (doi:10.1016/j.bandl.2009.05.002) and Whitehouse & Bishop (2008). Because shipped row 2411 captures only Whitehouse & Bishop (2008) (blind target 3), Illingworth & Bishop (2009) is a genuinely distinct missing replication target.

decisions.location: Methods, lines 1527-1535 (see also Results lines 2081-2107; References lines 2777-2785)
decisions.quote:
A subsidiary aim was to see whether we could replicate associations between language 

laterality and language tests found by Groen et al. (2012). Analysis was conducted in two 

replication samples, as described above, so that data from only one twin of each twin pair 

contributed to each analysis. Spearman's method was used, since the laterality index is not 

normally distributed, and all 13 language measures as well as performance IQ were included.
decisions.reason: Prior adjudication and state files are absent for this work. Both the Methods (lines 1527-1545) and Results (lines 2081-2107) explicitly state a subsidiary replication aim to re-test the continuous associations between fTCD language laterality and language test performance reported by Groen et al. (2012) (doi:10.1002/brb3.56) by computing Spearman's correlations across two twin replication subsamples. This is a distinct original study and empirical replication test not represented by shipped row 2411 (Whitehouse & Bishop, 2008) or any other sibling target.

corrected_value.title: Handedness and specific language impairment: A study of 6-year-old twins

decisions.location: Results, lines 1918-1926 (see also Methods lines 1453-1505; Discussion lines 2193-2201; References lines 2483-2487)
decisions.quote:
We also tested the hypothesis that children with DLD were less likely in the QHP task to 

reach across the midline with the right hand to a spatial position on the left side of the body, 

indicating weaker hand preference, as previously reported (Bishop, 2005; E. L. Hill & Bishop, 

1998). A multilevel model was run with twin pair membership as a random effect, group as a 

between factor and spatial position as a within factor.
decisions.reason: Prior adjudication and state files are absent for this work (never previously adjudicated). The source text explicitly re-tests the finding of Bishop (2005) (doi:10.1002/dev.20062) that developmental language disorder (SLI/DLD) is associated with a reduced tendency to reach across the midline with the right hand on the Quantification of Hand Preference (QHP) task. This empirical replication test is specified in Methods (lines 1453-1505), executed via multilevel modeling in Results (lines 1918-1960), and evaluated in the Discussion (lines 2193-2201). It is an independent original study (6-year-old twins in Developmental Psychobiology) distinct from shipped row 2411 (Whitehouse & Bishop, 2008, adult fTCD cerebral dominance) and from sibling target 1 (Hill & Bishop, 1998, clinical SLI/DCD sample in Laterality).

decisions.reason: Prior adjudication and state files are absent for this work. The source text explicitly states in Methods (lines 1453-1505), Results (lines 1918-1960), and Discussion (lines 2193-2201) that it attempts to replicate the previously reported association between language disorder and reduced right-hand reaching across the midline on the QHP task reported by Hill & Bishop (1998) (doi:10.1080/713754314). Although cited alongside Bishop (2005) (target 0), Hill & Bishop (1998) is an independent original study in a separate clinical sample of children with SLI and developmental coordination disorder rather than a same-study wave, and is not covered by shipped row 2411 (Whitehouse & Bishop, 2008).
